Ronald Reagan. On June 12, 1987, the president stood at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin and issued a direct challenge to Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. The Cold War seemed permanent, yet Reagan spoke as though it could end. His demand was simple and unforgettable: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall."

He framed the wall not as a mere structure but as a symbol of Communist oppression and European division. What kept it up, Reagan insisted, were lies and the repression of the people. He challenged Gorbachev: if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity, if you seek liberalization, then tear down this wall. The speech marked a shift in Reagan's tone—he was no longer merely confronting Soviet power but inviting it to reform.

The speech's historical resonance was enhanced by its prescience. When Reagan spoke these words, the Cold War appeared to have no end. Yet less than two years later, in November 1989, the wall fell. That moral and ideological victory vindicated Reagan's vision and made his speech a signature moment of his presidency. He had helped bring a long struggle to its close.
